Longitudinal data and mixed models
text: This page explains the model behind the repeated-measures outcomes (ACT, AQLQ, PACQLQ, AFS and self-reported adherence) in general terms. It says nothing about this trial’s results. The last methods page shows where each idea appears in the code.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
section: Why repeated measures need their own model
text:
Why repeated measures need their own model
In a trial with visits at baseline and at several follow-up times, each participant contributes several measurements. Measurements from the same person are more alike than measurements from different people: someone with well-controlled asthma at baseline tends to stay better controlled than average. A model that treats every row as independent overstates how much information the data hold, and its standard errors come out too small.
A linear mixed model handles this by giving each participant their own baseline level, a random intercept. The fixed effects describe the average course of each arm over time, and the random intercept absorbs each person’s persistent difference from that average. This is the model fitted with lme4 (Bates et al. 2015):


Click to show/hide R Code
# Each participant (study_id_screening) gets a random intercept
lmer(act_score ~ time_factor * studyarm + (1 | study_id_screening), data = visits)


A random intercept assumes that any two visits from the same person are equally correlated, however far apart they are. Richer structures (random slopes for time, or a correlation that falls off with distance) are possible, at the cost of more parameters.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
section: Time as a factor, not a line
text:
Time as a factor, not a line
time_factor treats each visit (0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12 months) as its own category, so the model estimates a separate mean for each arm at each visit without assuming a straight line or any other shape over time. With six visits that’s 12 means (6 visits × 2 arms). The price is more parameters than a linear trend; the gain is that a rise and then a fall, or an early change that levels off, are described as they are.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
text:
What the coefficients mean
With R’s default coding, control is the reference arm and baseline is the reference visit. The model time_factor * studyarm then has these fixed effects:







Coefficient
Meaning




(Intercept)
Mean in the control arm at baseline


studyarm1
Difference between arms at baseline


time_factor2, time_factor4, …
Change from baseline in the control arm at each visit


time_factor2:studyarm1, …
How much more (or less) the intervention arm changed from baseline than the control arm, at each visit



The last row matters most. Each visit-by-arm term is a difference in change from baseline: the arm difference at that visit minus the arm difference at baseline. This is what the plots mean by “adjusted for baseline differences”. In a randomized trial the baseline difference should be small, but subtracting it removes any chance imbalance from the comparison at later visits.
The arm difference at a given visit itself, with no baseline subtraction, is not one coefficient: it’s studyarm1 plus that visit’s interaction term. Adding a subgroup to this model is covered in Interactions. Getting such combinations, with their confidence intervals, is the subject of Effects behind an interaction.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
text:
Missed visits
A mixed model uses every visit a participant attended, even if they missed others. That’s a real advantage over analyses that keep only people with complete data. The estimates are unbiased if missing visits are missing at random: whether a visit is missed may depend on the person’s earlier, observed values, but not on the value that would have been measured. If people tended to miss visits because they were doing badly at that moment, the model can’t detect it, and the estimates would be biased.

title: Longitudinal data and mixed models
text:
Count outcomes are different
The 12-month health care use counts and the rescue inhaler counts are one value per participant, not repeated measures, so they don’t need a mixed model. They are fitted with negative binomial regression on the log scale, with the log of each person’s follow-up time as an offset, so the model describes rates (events per day of follow-up) rather than raw counts. On the log scale, exponentiated coefficients are incidence rate ratios: an arm effect of 0.8 means the intervention arm’s rate is 80% of the control arm’s.

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text: This page explains what the p-value of an interaction term tests, and what it doesn’t. It uses no results from this trial.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
section: It tests a difference between effects
text:
It tests a difference between effects
The p-value of an arm × subgroup interaction tests one null hypothesis: the arm effect is the same in every level of the subgroup. A small p-value is evidence that the effects differ. It is not a test of whether the intervention works in any one subgroup.
Altman and Bland make the general point: to compare two estimates, test their difference directly; don’t compare their separate p-values (Altman and Bland 2003).
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
section: “Significant in one subgroup and not the other” is not evidence of a difference
text:
“Significant in one subgroup and not the other” is not evidence of a difference
A common mistake is to fit the model in each subgroup separately, find p < 0.05 in one and p > 0.05 in the other, and conclude the intervention works only in the first. Two estimates can be almost identical while one crosses 0.05 and the other doesn’t, especially when the subgroups differ in size. Brookes and colleagues showed by simulation how often subgroup-specific tests produce this pattern when the true effect is the same in both groups, and that the interaction test is the right comparison (Brookes et al. 2004).
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
It has low power
A trial sized to detect the overall effect has far less power to detect an interaction of the same size. In Brookes and colleagues’ simulations, a trial with 80% power for the overall effect had only about 29% power for an interaction of that magnitude, and roughly four times the sample size was needed to match (Brookes et al. 2004). In a pilot trial this matters even more: a large p-value for interaction is weak evidence that the effects are the same.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
It depends on the scale
As the Interactions page explains, an interaction is measured on a scale. A test on the ratio scale (count models) and a test on the difference scale (mixed models) are answering different questions, and can disagree on the same data.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
text:
Many tests
Each subgroup variable, outcome, population and visit adds tests. With several subgroups, several outcomes, two populations and an interaction p-value at every visit, some small p-values are expected by chance alone. Wang and colleagues’ guidance on reporting subgroup analyses asks that the number of subgroup analyses be stated, that prespecified and post hoc analyses be distinguished, and that interaction tests rather than subgroup-specific tests be the basis for claims of different effects (Wang et al. 2007). In this analysis every subgroup analysis is post hoc and none is adjusted for multiplicity (see the analysis plan).
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

title: What a p-value for interaction means
section: Report the effects, not only the p-value
text:
Report the effects, not only the p-value
Because the interaction p-value says nothing about the size of the effect in each group, it’s best reported alongside the effect within each subgroup level, with its confidence interval (Knol and VanderWeele 2012). Effects behind an interaction shows how to get those.
crumbs: What a p-value for interaction means

text:
Create ME plot
Inside, the function refits the same model in three codings (models A, B and C) to read off cell means and contrasts; How this code does it explains each one, and Effects behind an interaction the method behind model C.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Spaghetti plot of an outcome over time by arm: individual trajectories,
# model-estimated means with 95% confidence intervals, numbers observed, and
# p values for the arm difference at each visit. With an interaction
# variable (a two-level factor), one panel per level plus a row of p values
# for the difference between levels, combined with patchwork. The function
# refits its own models; see the efficiency issue.
create_me_plot <- function(trial_data, outcome_of_interest,
                           interaction_variable = NULL,
                           plot_title = "Plot") {
  if (is.null(interaction_variable)) {
    # Top of the plot
    y_max <- trial_data %>%
      select(all_of(outcome_of_interest)) %>%
      max(., na.rm = TRUE) + 3

    lmer_formula_1 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest, "~time_factor*studyarm+(1|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()
    lmer_formula_2 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest, "~ me_factor-1 + (1|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()

    # Mixed model with time as a factor: p values for the arm difference
    mixed_model_a <- lmer(lmer_formula_1, data = trial_data)

    # Same model, parameterized by visit-by-arm cell: no p values for the
    # arm difference, but a mean and confidence interval for each cell
    mixed_model_b <- lmer(lmer_formula_2, data = trial_data)

    mixed_model_a_p_values <- mixed_model_a %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      filter(str_detect(term, "studyarm")) %>%
      mutate(time_linear = case_when(
        str_detect(term, "time_factor2") == TRUE ~ 2,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor4") == TRUE ~ 4,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor6") == TRUE ~ 6,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor9") == TRUE ~ 9,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor12") == TRUE ~ 12,
        TRUE ~ 0
      )) %>%
      mutate(p.value = round(p.value, 3)) %>%
      mutate(p_value_label = paste0("p=", p.value)) %>%
      mutate(p_value_label = ifelse(
        time_linear == 0,
        p_value_label,
        paste0(p_value_label, "†")
      )) %>%
      select(time_linear, p_value_label)

    # Cell means from model B. Terms read "me_factortime_<t>_studyarm_<a>":
    # the extra NA allows for the underscore in "me_factor".
    mixed_model_predictions <- mixed_model_b %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
      filter(str_detect(term, "time")) %>%
      separate(
        term,
        sep = "_",
        into = c(NA, NA, "time_linear", NA, "studyarm")
      ) %>%
      mutate(time_factor = (as.factor(time_linear))) %>%
      mutate(studyarm = as_factor(studyarm)) %>%
      mutate(time_linear = as.numeric(time_linear)) %>%
      mutate(time_linear_shifted = ifelse(
        studyarm == "1",
        time_linear + 0.25,
        time_linear - 0.25
      ))

    # Number observed in each arm at each visit
    mixed_model_predictions <- trial_data %>%
      filter(!is.na(get(outcome_of_interest))) %>%
      group_by(time_linear, studyarm) %>%
      summarize(n_obs = n()) %>%
      left_join(
        .,
        mixed_model_predictions,
        by = c("time_linear", "studyarm")
      )

    # Spaghetti plot with model means over individual trajectories
    ggplot() +
      geom_point(
        trial_data,
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = get(outcome_of_interest),
          color = studyarm, group = study_id_screening
        ),
        alpha = 0.2
      ) +
      geom_line(
        trial_data,
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = get(outcome_of_interest),
          color = studyarm, group = study_id_screening
        ),
        alpha = 0.2
      ) +
      geom_point(
        mixed_model_predictions,
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear_shifted, y = estimate, color = studyarm),
        size = 2
      ) +
      geom_line(
        mixed_model_predictions,
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = estimate, color = studyarm,
          group = studyarm
        ),
        size = 2
      ) +
      geom_errorbar(
        mixed_model_predictions,
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high,
          color = studyarm
        ),
        size = 1.5
      ) +
      theme_bw() +
      geom_text(
        filter(mixed_model_predictions, studyarm == 1),
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = 0, label = n_obs, color = studyarm)
      ) +
      geom_text(
        filter(mixed_model_predictions, studyarm == 0),
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = 1, label = n_obs, color = studyarm)
      ) +
      geom_text(mapping = aes(x = -0.5, y = 1, label = "N")) +
      geom_text(
        mixed_model_a_p_values,
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = y_max, label = p_value_label)
      ) +
      scale_x_continuous(
        breaks = c(0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12),
        limits = c(-0.5, 12.5),
        minor_breaks = 0:12
      ) +
      ylab(outcome_of_interest) +
      xlab("Time (months)") +
      scale_color_discrete(
        name = "Study Arm",
        labels = c("Control", "Treatment")
      ) +
      labs(caption = "† adjusted for baseline differences") +
      theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.0555)) +
      ggtitle(plot_title)
  } else {
    # The interaction variable must be a two-level factor
    plot_labels <- trial_data %>%
      pull(interaction_variable) %>%
      levels()
    y_max <- trial_data %>%
      select(all_of(outcome_of_interest)) %>%
      max(., na.rm = TRUE) + 3

    data_for_function <- trial_data %>%
      mutate(interaction_variable_numeric = factor(
        as.numeric(get(interaction_variable))
      )) %>%
      mutate(me_factor_interaction_variable = paste(
        "time", time_linear, "studyarm", studyarm, interaction_variable,
        interaction_variable_numeric,
        sep = "__"
      ))

    # Formulas 1 and 2 are defined but not fitted
    lmer_formula_1 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest,
      "~time_linear*studyarm*interaction_variable_numeric",
      "+(1|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()
    lmer_formula_2 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest,
      "~time_linear*studyarm*interaction_variable_numeric",
      "+(time_linear|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()
    lmer_formula_3 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest,
      "~time_factor*studyarm*interaction_variable_numeric",
      "+(1|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()
    lmer_formula_4 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest,
      " ~ me_factor_interaction_variable-1 + (1|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()
    lmer_formula_5 <- paste0(
      outcome_of_interest,
      "~interaction_variable_numeric-1 + ",
      "interaction_variable_numeric:time_factor + ",
      "interaction_variable_numeric:studyarm + ",
      "time_factor:studyarm:interaction_variable_numeric +",
      "(1|study_id_screening)"
    ) %>%
      as.formula()

    # Model A, time as a factor: p values for the difference in arm effect
    # between levels of the interaction variable
    mixed_model_a_interaction <- lmer(
      lmer_formula_3,
      data = data_for_function
    )

    mixed_model_a_heterogeneity <- mixed_model_a_interaction %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      filter(str_detect(term, "studyarm")) %>%
      filter(str_detect(term, "interaction_variable_numeric")) %>%
      mutate(time_linear = case_when(
        str_detect(term, "time_factor2") == TRUE ~ 2,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor4") == TRUE ~ 4,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor6") == TRUE ~ 6,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor9") == TRUE ~ 9,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor12") == TRUE ~ 12,
        TRUE ~ 0
      )) %>%
      mutate(p.value = round(p.value, 3)) %>%
      mutate(p_value_label = paste0("p=", p.value)) %>%
      select(time_linear, p_value_label)

    # Model B, parameterized by cell: a mean and confidence interval for each
    # visit, arm and level
    mixed_model_b_interaction <- lmer(
      lmer_formula_4,
      data = data_for_function
    )

    # (In the original, a table of model B, printed inside the function and
    # not returned)
    mixed_model_b_interaction %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      flextable()

    # Summary statistics confirm model B is the same model as A
    glance(mixed_model_b_interaction)

    # Model C, parameterized for the arm difference within each level
    mixed_model_c_interaction <- lmer(
      lmer_formula_5,
      data = data_for_function
    )

    # (In the original, a table of model C, printed inside the function and
    # not returned)
    mixed_model_c_interaction %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      flextable()

    # Summary statistics confirm model C is the same model as A
    glance(mixed_model_c_interaction)

    # P values from model C, nested by level
    mixed_model_c_treatment_effect <- mixed_model_c_interaction %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      filter(str_detect(term, "studyarm")) %>%
      mutate(interaction_variable = case_when(
        str_detect(term, "interaction_variable_numeric1") == TRUE ~ 1,
        str_detect(term, "interaction_variable_numeric2") == TRUE ~ 2
      )) %>%
      mutate(time_linear = case_when(
        str_detect(term, "time_factor2") == TRUE ~ 2,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor4") == TRUE ~ 4,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor6") == TRUE ~ 6,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor9") == TRUE ~ 9,
        str_detect(term, "time_factor12") == TRUE ~ 12,
        TRUE ~ 0
      )) %>%
      mutate(p.value = round(p.value, 3)) %>%
      mutate(p_value_label = paste0("p=", p.value)) %>%
      mutate(p_value_label = ifelse(
        time_linear == 0,
        p_value_label,
        paste0(p_value_label, "†")
      )) %>%
      select(interaction_variable, time_linear, p_value_label) %>%
      group_by(interaction_variable) %>%
      nest()

    # Cell means from model B
    predictions_interaction <- mixed_model_b_interaction %>%
      tidy(., conf.int = TRUE) %>%
      select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
      filter(str_detect(term, "time")) %>%
      separate(
        term,
        sep = "__",
        into = c(NA, "time_linear", NA, "studyarm", NA, "interaction_term")
      ) %>%
      mutate(time_factor = (as.factor(time_linear))) %>%
      mutate(studyarm = as_factor(studyarm)) %>%
      mutate(time_linear = as.numeric(time_linear)) %>%
      mutate(time_linear_shifted_1 = case_when(
        studyarm == "0" & interaction_term == "1" ~ time_linear - 0.5,
        studyarm == "1" & interaction_term == "1" ~ time_linear - 0.25,
        studyarm == "0" & interaction_term == "2" ~ time_linear + 0.25,
        studyarm == "1" & interaction_term == "2" ~ time_linear + 0.5
      )) %>%
      mutate(time_linear_shifted_2 = case_when(
        studyarm == "0" & interaction_term == "1" ~ time_linear - 0.25,
        studyarm == "1" & interaction_term == "1" ~ time_linear + 0.25,
        studyarm == "0" & interaction_term == "2" ~ time_linear - 0.25,
        studyarm == "1" & interaction_term == "2" ~ time_linear + 0.25
      )) %>%
      mutate(interaction_variable = as.factor(interaction_term)) %>%
      select(-interaction_term)

    # Number observed in each arm and level at each visit
    predictions_interaction <- data_for_function %>%
      filter(!is.na(get(outcome_of_interest))) %>%
      group_by(time_linear, studyarm, interaction_variable_numeric) %>%
      summarize(n_obs = n()) %>%
      rename(interaction_variable = interaction_variable_numeric) %>%
      left_join(
        .,
        predictions_interaction,
        by = c("time_linear", "studyarm", "interaction_variable")
      ) %>%
      group_by(studyarm, interaction_variable) %>%
      mutate(gid = cur_group_id())

    # Data and predictions nested by level
    data_nested_interaction <- data_for_function %>%
      group_by(interaction_variable_numeric) %>%
      nest() %>%
      rename(interaction_variable = interaction_variable_numeric)

    predictions_nested_interaction <- predictions_interaction %>%
      group_by(interaction_variable) %>%
      nest()

    # (In the original, the predictions table, printed inside the function
    # and not returned)
    predictions_interaction %>% flextable()

    # Panel for the first level
    plot_level_1 <- ggplot() +
      geom_point(
        data_nested_interaction$data[[1]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = get(outcome_of_interest),
          color = studyarm, group = study_id_screening
        ),
        alpha = 0.2
      ) +
      geom_line(
        data_nested_interaction$data[[1]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = get(outcome_of_interest),
          color = studyarm, group = study_id_screening
        ),
        alpha = 0.2
      ) +
      geom_point(
        predictions_nested_interaction$data[[1]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted_2, y = estimate, color = studyarm
        ),
        size = 2
      ) +
      geom_line(
        predictions_nested_interaction$data[[1]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted_2, y = estimate, color = studyarm,
          group = gid
        ),
        size = 2
      ) +
      theme_bw() +
      geom_text(
        filter(
          predictions_interaction,
          studyarm == 0,
          interaction_variable == 1
        ),
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = 1, label = n_obs, color = studyarm)
      ) +
      geom_text(
        filter(
          predictions_interaction,
          studyarm == 1,
          interaction_variable == 1
        ),
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = -1, label = n_obs, color = studyarm)
      ) +
      geom_text(mapping = aes(x = -1, y = 1, label = "N")) +
      geom_text(mapping = aes(x = -1, y = -1, label = plot_labels[1])) +
      geom_text(
        mixed_model_c_treatment_effect$data[[1]],
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = y_max, label = p_value_label)
      ) +
      geom_errorbar(
        predictions_nested_interaction$data[[1]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted_2, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high,
          color = studyarm
        ),
        size = 1.5
      ) +
      scale_x_continuous(
        breaks = NULL,
        limits = c(-1, 12.5),
        minor_breaks = 0:12
      ) +
      scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-3, y_max)) +
      theme(axis.title.x = element_blank()) +
      ylab(outcome_of_interest) +
      scale_color_discrete(
        name = "Study Arm",
        labels = c("Control", "Treatment")
      )

    # Panel for the second level
    plot_level_2 <- ggplot() +
      geom_point(
        data_nested_interaction$data[[2]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = get(outcome_of_interest),
          color = studyarm, group = study_id_screening
        ),
        alpha = 0.2
      ) +
      geom_line(
        data_nested_interaction$data[[2]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted, y = get(outcome_of_interest),
          color = studyarm, group = study_id_screening
        ),
        alpha = 0.2
      ) +
      geom_point(
        predictions_nested_interaction$data[[2]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted_2, y = estimate, color = studyarm
        ),
        size = 2
      ) +
      geom_line(
        predictions_nested_interaction$data[[2]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted_2, y = estimate, color = studyarm,
          group = gid
        ),
        size = 2
      ) +
      theme_bw() +
      geom_text(
        filter(
          predictions_interaction,
          studyarm == 0,
          interaction_variable == 2
        ),
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = 1, label = n_obs, color = studyarm)
      ) +
      geom_text(
        filter(
          predictions_interaction,
          studyarm == 1,
          interaction_variable == 2
        ),
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = -1, label = n_obs, color = studyarm)
      ) +
      geom_text(mapping = aes(x = -1, y = 1, label = "N")) +
      geom_text(mapping = aes(x = -1, y = -1, label = plot_labels[2])) +
      geom_text(
        mixed_model_c_treatment_effect$data[[2]],
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = y_max, label = p_value_label)
      ) +
      geom_errorbar(
        predictions_nested_interaction$data[[2]],
        mapping = aes(
          x = time_linear_shifted_2, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high,
          color = studyarm
        ),
        size = 1.5
      ) +
      scale_x_continuous(
        breaks = NULL,
        limits = c(-1, 12.5),
        minor_breaks = 0:12
      ) +
      scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-3, y_max)) +
      theme(axis.title.x = element_blank()) +
      ylab(outcome_of_interest) +
      scale_color_discrete(
        name = "Study Arm",
        labels = c("Control", "Treatment")
      )

    # Row of p values for the difference between levels
    plot_p_values <- ggplot() +
      geom_text(
        data = mixed_model_a_heterogeneity,
        mapping = aes(x = time_linear, y = 0, label = p_value_label)
      ) +
      theme_void() +
      scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1, 12.5))

    # Combine the panels with patchwork
    plot_level_1 / plot_level_2 / plot_p_values +
      plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(0.48, 0.48, 0.04)) +
      plot_annotation(
        title = plot_title,
        caption = "† adjusted for baseline differences",
        theme = theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.0555))
      )
  }
}

title: How this code does it
text: This page maps the ideas on the other methods pages to the analysis code, as it stands now, and notes what is planned to change.

title: How this code does it
text:
Mixed-model tables: create_me_table()
create_me_table() fits outcome ~ time_factor * studyarm + (1 | study_id_screening), or the three-way version with a subgroup, and returns the model’s coefficients as a table. 5. Fit mixed models calls it 56 times: 5 outcomes overall, 5 outcomes × 4 subgroups, and 3 outcomes by child or adult, each in the intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations.
So the tables show the raw coefficients described on Longitudinal data and mixed models and Interactions: the baseline arm difference, the change-from-baseline differences at each visit, and the interaction terms. They don’t show the arm effect in each subgroup level directly.

title: How this code does it
text:
Mixed-model plots: create_me_plot()
create_me_plot() draws the same analyses, called from Figures for the same 56 analyses. Inside, it refits the model in up to three codings, each chosen to make different numbers appear directly as coefficients:








Inside the function
Coding
What it’s used for




Model A
time_factor * studyarm (times the subgroup)
The p-values printed above each visit: the change-from-baseline arm differences (marked †), or, with a subgroup, the differences between levels


Model B
One coefficient per visit-by-arm cell (me_factor - 1)
Each cell’s mean and confidence interval, the points and bars on the plot


Model C, subgroups only
The arm effect nested within each level
The p-values printed in each level’s panel: the baseline arm difference and the change-from-baseline arm differences within that level



All three are the same model: they fit identically and differ only in which combinations of the fitted values they report. Model C is the “refit with a different coding” approach from Effects behind an interaction, so the subgroup plots already show the arm effect within each level, which the tables don’t.

title: How this code does it
text:
Count models
4. Fit count models fits negative binomial models with log follow-up time as the offset, overall and with each arm × subgroup interaction, and reports exponentiated coefficients: IRRs, and for the interaction terms, ratios of IRRs. As with the mixed-model tables, the IRR in the non-reference level of a subgroup isn’t shown directly.

title: How this code does it
text:
What is planned to change

#10: fit each model once and pass it to both the table and the plot, taking cell means and contrasts with emmeans instead of refitting in other codings.
#8: move all tables to gtsummary, and decide whether to report the effects within each subgroup level, the interaction terms, or both.
#9: the examples on Effects behind an interaction, run on synthetic data where the true effects are known.

title: Interactions
text: This page explains what the coefficients of a model with an interaction mean, for the two kinds of model this analysis uses. It uses made-up numbers only.

title: Interactions
text:
Effect modification in a trial
A subgroup analysis asks whether the intervention’s effect differs between groups of participants: by preferred language, sex, child or adult, or baseline adherence or asthma control. The usual way to ask it is to add an arm × subgroup interaction to the model. The interaction lets the arm effect take a different value in each subgroup level.

title: Interactions
text:
Reading the coefficients: count models
For a count outcome with a two-level subgroup (say English and Spanish, with English as the reference level):


Click to show/hide R Code
glm.nb(
  rescue_puffs_itt ~ studyarm * prefer_language + offset(log(followup_time_itt)),
  data = participants
)


On the log scale, and after exponentiating:







Exponentiated coefficient
Meaning




studyarm1
Incidence rate ratio (IRR), intervention vs control, in the reference level only (English)


prefer_languageSpanish
Rate ratio, Spanish vs English, in the control arm only


studyarm1:prefer_languageSpanish
Ratio of the two IRRs: IRR in Spanish speakers ÷ IRR in English speakers



So a table of these terms never shows the arm effect in the second level directly. With made-up numbers: if studyarm1 is 0.80 and the interaction is 1.25, the IRR in English speakers is 0.80 and the IRR in Spanish speakers is 0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00. The interaction of 1.25 isn’t an effect in anyone; it’s how much the effect changes between levels.

title: Interactions
section: Reading the coefficients: linear mixed models

title: Interactions
text:
Scale matters
An interaction is always measured on a scale. The count models are multiplicative (a ratio of IRRs); the mixed models are additive (a difference of differences). The same data can show an interaction on one scale and none on the other. For example, rates of 2 and 1 in one subgroup and 4 and 2 in another have the same ratio (2) in both, so no multiplicative interaction, but different differences (1 and 2), so an additive one. Knol and VanderWeele recommend reporting the effect within each stratum alongside interaction measures, so readers can judge both (Knol and VanderWeele 2012).

title: Figures
Effects behind an interaction
text: A model with an interaction holds the arm effect for every subgroup level and every visit, but its coefficients show only some of them directly (see Interactions). This page shows two ways to get all of them, with confidence intervals, from a model already fitted. Both give the same answer. The code is shown, not run, and uses illustrative object names.

title: Effects behind an interaction
text:
By hand from the coefficients
The arm effect in a non-reference level is a sum of coefficients, so its variance is a sum of variances and covariances. For the count model rescue_puffs_itt ~ studyarm * prefer_language + offset(...):
\[
\log \text{IRR}_{\text{Spanish}} = \beta_{\text{arm}} + \beta_{\text{arm} \times \text{Spanish}}
\]
\[
\text{Var} = \text{Var}(\beta_{\text{arm}}) + \text{Var}(\beta_{\text{arm} \times \text{Spanish}}) + 2\,\text{Cov}(\beta_{\text{arm}}, \beta_{\text{arm} \times \text{Spanish}})
\]


Click to show/hide R Code
b <- coef(fit)
v <- vcov(fit)
terms <- c("studyarm1", "studyarm1:prefer_languageSpanish")

log_irr <- sum(b[terms])
se <- sqrt(sum(v[terms, terms]))     # the sum of the 2 x 2 block

exp(log_irr)                          # IRR in Spanish speakers
exp(log_irr + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se)


The same idea works for any combination: the arm difference at the 6-month visit in one subgroup level of a mixed model is the sum of the baseline arm term and the relevant two- and three-way terms.

title: Effects behind an interaction
section: By refitting with a different reference level
text:
By refitting with a different reference level
The coefficient for studyarm1 is the arm effect in the reference level, so making the other level the reference gives its effect directly:


Click to show/hide R Code
participants_spanish_ref <- participants %>%
  mutate(prefer_language = relevel(prefer_language, ref = "Spanish"))

fit_spanish_ref <- glm.nb(
  rescue_puffs_itt ~ studyarm * prefer_language + offset(log(followup_time_itt)),
  data = participants_spanish_ref
)
# exp(coef(fit_spanish_ref)["studyarm1"]) is now the IRR in Spanish speakers


This is the same model, coded differently: it fits identically, and the interaction p-value doesn’t change. Recoding the reference level this way is also what the plotting function’s “model C” does (see How this code does it).

title: Effects behind an interaction
text:
With emmeans
emmeans computes these combinations from the fitted model, without refitting and without writing out terms by hand (Lenth and Piaskowski 2026). For the count model:


Click to show/hide R Code
library(emmeans)

emmeans(fit, ~ studyarm | prefer_language, type = "response") %>%
  contrast("revpairwise")


This gives one row per language: the intervention-vs-control IRR (a ratio column) with its confidence interval. On the log scale, comparisons are differences of logs, which become ratios when back-transformed. Both arms are compared at the same follow-up time, so the offset cancels out of the ratio.
For the mixed model, the arm difference at each visit within each subgroup level:


Click to show/hide R Code
emmeans(fit_lmer, ~ studyarm | time_factor * prefer_language) %>%
  contrast("revpairwise")


These are differences on the score scale, with no baseline subtraction. To get the change-from-baseline differences that the model’s interaction terms describe, ask for an interaction contrast between arms and between each visit and baseline:


Click to show/hide R Code
emmeans(fit_lmer, ~ studyarm * time_factor | prefer_language) %>%
  contrast(interaction = c("revpairwise", "trt.vs.ctrl"))


For lmer models, emmeans chooses its own degrees-of-freedom method (Kenward–Roger or Satterthwaite; see its documentation), so p-values can differ slightly from the ones lmerTest reports.

title: Effects behind an interaction
text:
Check that the methods agree
On synthetic data, the hand calculation, the refit with a new reference level and emmeans should give the same estimate and, for the count models, the same confidence interval. Showing that is a good test that the right terms were combined. These calls are checked against emmeans’ help pages for the installed version before they’re used in the analysis.

title: 2. Build visit data
text:
Build visit data


Click to show/hide R Code
clean_asthma_data_itt <- clean_asthma_data %>%
  # Months since baseline for each REDCap event
  mutate(time_linear = case_when(
    redcap_event_name == "baseline_arm_1" ~ 0,
    redcap_event_name == "2month_followup_arm_1" ~ 2,
    redcap_event_name == "4month_followup_arm_1" ~ 4,
    redcap_event_name == "6month_followup_arm_1" ~ 6,
    redcap_event_name == "9month_followup_arm_1" ~ 9,
    redcap_event_name == "12month_followup_arm_1" ~ 12
  )) %>%
  # A preferred language of 999 is set to English. See issue #16.
  mutate(prefer_language = ifelse(
    prefer_language == 999,
    1,
    prefer_language
  )) %>%
  # Visit time as a factor, for models that treat time as categorical
  mutate(time_factor = as_factor(time_linear)) %>%
  mutate(studyarm = as.factor(studyarm)) %>%
  mutate(participant_sex = factor(
    participant_sex,
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("Male", "Female")
  )) %>%
  mutate(child_adult = factor(
    child_adult,
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("Child", "Adult")
  )) %>%
  mutate(prefer_language = factor(
    prefer_language,
    levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c("English", "Spanish")
  )) %>%
  # These are recorded only at baseline; carry them to every visit
  group_by(study_id_screening) %>%
  fill(
    studyarm, child_adult, prefer_language, consent_date,
    follow_up_2_months, follow_up_4_months, follow_up_6_months,
    follow_up_9_months, follow_up_12_month
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(across(
    all_of(c(aqlq_items, pacqlq_items, afs_items, missing_999_variables)),
    ~ ifelse(.x == 999, NA, .x)
  )) %>%
  # Date of each visit, from the consent and follow-up dates
  mutate(date_of_observation = case_when(
    redcap_event_name == "baseline_arm_1" ~ consent_date,
    redcap_event_name == "2month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_2_months,
    redcap_event_name == "4month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_4_months,
    redcap_event_name == "6month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_6_months,
    redcap_event_name == "9month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_9_months,
    redcap_event_name == "12month_followup_arm_1" ~ follow_up_12_month
  )) %>%
  # Visits after the app update glitch
  mutate(post_glitch_date = (date_of_observation > glitch_date)) %>%
  # Visit-by-arm cell label, and a time offset so arms do not overlap in plots
  mutate(me_factor = paste(
    "time", time_linear, "studyarm", studyarm,
    sep = "_"
  )) %>%
  mutate(time_linear_shifted = ifelse(
    studyarm == 1,
    time_linear + 0.1,
    time_linear - 0.1
  )) %>%
  # Self-reported controller adherence score. See analysis-plan.md.
  mutate(self_reported_adherence = 32 -
    only_give_controller_medication_needed -
    only_give_controller_medication_breathless +
    give_controller_medication_regularly -
    try_to_avoid_controller_medication -
    forget_give_controller_medication -
    alter_change_dosage_controller_medication -
    stop_giving_controller_medication -
    reserve_controller_medication_if_treatment_not_work -
    give_controller_medication_child_does_breathless +
    give_controller_medication_as_label) %>%
  # Baseline adherence and asthma control groups, carried to every visit
  mutate(self_reported_adherence_binary = case_when(
    self_reported_adherence >= adherence_cutoff &
      time_factor == "0" ~ "Adherent",
    self_reported_adherence < adherence_cutoff &
      time_factor == "0" ~ "Non-adherent"
  )) %>%
  mutate(
    self_reported_adherence_binary = as.factor(self_reported_adherence_binary)
  ) %>%
  mutate(act_binary = case_when(
    act_score >= act_cutoff & time_factor == "0" ~ "Controlled",
    act_score < act_cutoff & time_factor == "0" ~ "Uncontrolled"
  )) %>%
  mutate(act_binary = as.factor(act_binary)) %>%
  group_by(study_id_screening) %>%
  fill(self_reported_adherence_binary, act_binary) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Each score is the mean of the items answered at that visit
  mutate(aqlq_score = rowMeans(across(all_of(aqlq_items)), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(
    pacqlq_score = rowMeans(across(all_of(pacqlq_items)), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(afs_score = rowMeans(across(all_of(afs_items)), na.rm = TRUE))
